background.definition: Any decreased ability to hear is considered a hearing loss. Practically speaking, hearing loss is often considered when there is a pure-tone threshold of 25 dB or greater.

list.listitem: In the National Health Interview Survey, approximately 17% of Americans older than 18 years report some hearing difficulty.
The prevalence increases with age: in adults younger than 45 years it equals 8%; between the ages of 45 and 64 years: 19%; between the ages of 65 and 74 years: 32%; and 75 years and older: 50%.
Hearing loss can negatively affect the patient’s quality of life.
Hearing loss may be associated with depression/social withdrawal, especially in elderly patients.
It is also associated cross-sectionally with frailty, although directionality cannot be established of this association.
Causes of hearing loss are summarized in .
Sensorineural hearing loss involves the inner ear and/or auditory nerve. It is more common and is usually permanent.

On the basis of case reports, there is a potential link between phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (used for erectile dysfunction and pulmonary artery hypertension) and sudden sensorineural hearing loss; withdrawal of the drug resolves or improves hearing loss in some.
Conductive hearing loss involves the external and/or middle ear structures (anything preventing sound from reaching the inner ear).
Mixed hearing loss is a combination of conductive and sensorineural causes.
There is evidence that genetic factors contribute to age-related hearing loss; heritability estimates for presbycusis adjusted for age, sex, education level, and work noise exposure exceed 50%.
There is no evidence that COVID-19 vaccination causes hearing loss.
Varies according to cause or type of hearing loss.
It may be inflammatory for many autoimmune processes, involve infarction of associated neurologic pathways, demyelination, or destruction of inner ear structure or nerve pathway in many infections.
Some ototoxic drugs may destroy hair cells in the cochlea; however, the exact mechanism is unknown for many drugs.
It may also involve mechanical obstruction as in conductive causes such as cerumen impaction or growth in the middle ear.

In a population-based survey, individuals with moderate to severe hearing loss had a significantly higher likelihood of reporting previous stroke (OR 2.04; 95% CI, 1.20-3.49) after multivariable adjustment. Moderate to severe hearing loss did not predict incident stroke after 5-year follow-up.
The USPSTF found insufficient evidence to assess the balance of benefits and harms of screening for hearing loss in asymptomatic adults aged 50 years or older. C
The USPSTF found insufficient evidence to assess the balance of benefits and harms of screening for hearing loss in asymptomatic adults aged 50 years or older.

A systematic review found no direct evidence that screening for hearing loss results in improvements in hearing-related function, but screening was associated with increased hearing aid use in one randomized trial.

Evaluation with otoscope and audiometry is recommended if the person has evidence of impaired hearing. At-risk workers should be screened for noise-induced hearing loss according to existing programs and occupational medicine guidelines.

Simple questions: one global question about current hearing loss such as "Do you have a hearing problem now?" or "Do you feel you have a hearing loss?" or a standardized screening questionnaire such as the Hearing Handicap Inventory in the Elderly-screening version can quickly screen at the point of care.
A smartphone self-test audiometry app was 91% sensitive and 94% specific comopared to reference audiometry in a low income community clinic in South Africa.

Advise patients to use noise protection. Unfortunately, studies on personal hearing protection have not been shown to reduce hearing loss to levels of non-noise exposed workers and hearing loss prevention programs, while successful in reducing noise exposure, have not been uniformly successful in preventing hearing loss. Some educational interventions have been successful in improving use of hearing protection devices.
Immunize patients against infections that can cause hearing loss and other complications (eg, mumps/measles/rubella, meningococcus, pneumococcus).
Avoid ototoxic medications (eg, aminoglycosides, aspirin, furosemide) when possible or use the lowest dose possible when they are needed.
In any patient with a complaint of hearing loss, thoroughly evaluate both clinically and audiometrically if no easily reversible cause is identified (ie, cerumen or infection). C

Bedside hearing tests have good specificity but poor sensitivity for detecting hearing loss, so if hearing loss is suspected or reported, refer patients for formal audiometry. The exception to this may be for the calibrated finger rub auditory screening test. B
Formal audiometry with hearing thresholds or pure tone audiogram is necessary for accurate diagnosis of the presence of hearing loss. B
Sudden hearing loss warrants urgent evaluation and treatment by a specialist. C
Hearing loss is often defined as a pure-tone threshold of 25 dB or greater in certain frequencies (often 500, 1000, and 2000 Hz).
There is no clear consensus, however, and some authorities use thresholds from 15 to 40 dB to indicate hearing impairment. Some also use additional frequencies in testing (250-8000 Hz).

When taking the history, address the time course of symptoms (acute vs chronic), associated symptoms such as tinnitus, pain, vertigo, and discharge, recent or previous trauma, family history, recent illness, and other ear, nose, and throat symptoms.

When doing the physical examination, focus on ear, nose, and throat including external ear structures, external auditory canal (cerumen, tumors or other obstruction), tympanic membrane (perforations, sclerosis/scar, retractions, effusions), and pneumoscopy. Also examine neck, chest, and other relevant systems to evaluate for associated conditions.
Audiologic evaluation: may use whispered voice testing, or global question regarding hearing loss, or audio scope and/or send directly for formal audiometry.

Other "bedside" tests including whispered voice testing, finger-rub, watch tick, and tuning fork testing are also used and have high specificity but poor sensitivity (few false positives, many false negatives). When hearing loss is suspected, refer for audiometry even if bedside tests are negative.

One study found use of a calibrated finger rub auditory screening test (strong finger rub) had high sensitivity (99%) and specificity (100%) for detecting hearing impairment with a negative likelihood ratio less than 0.1.
Formal audiometry with hearing thresholds or pure tone audiogram is necessary for accurate diagnosis of the presence of hearing loss.

Formal diagnosis of hearing impairment requires formal audiologic testing by trained professionals using standardized equipment in soundproof rooms or booths. Formal audiometric testing allows accurate diagnosis of the type, degree, and frequencies of the hearing loss and is necessary for proper treatment. Pure tone, bone and air conduction, and speech/word discrimination are usually tested. Thresholds are obtained.

Consider MRI (with and without contrast) of the internal auditory canal and posterior fossa to rule out acoustic neuroma or other tumors, particularly if unilateral or progressive hearing loss is present.
CT should not be routinely performed for sudden hearing loss. CT is recommended in patients with conductive hearing loss if petrous bone abnormality is suspected.
Consider laboratory testing (CBC with differential, thyroid-stimulating hormone tests for syphilis, glucose) particularly for sensorineural hearing loss.
A smartphone self-test audiometry app was 91% sensitive and 94% specific comopared to reference audiometry in a low income community clinic in South Africa.
Perform a thorough history and physical examination of the ear, followed by a screening audiogram in the office if available.

Refer for formal audiometry and/or ear, nose, and throat evaluation if the cause of hearing loss is undetermined, if office testing is unavailable or inconclusive, and when hearing loss is not caused by an easily treated condition, such as cerumen impaction.
In patients with sensorineural hearing loss, order CT or MRI of the internal auditory canal and posterior fossa, particularly if loss is unilateral or progressive.
Sudden hearing loss is considered a medical emergency/urgency and requires urgent evaluation by an otolaryngologist.

feature.caption: Causes of Hearing Loss (in Alphabetical Order).
feature.feature_body:
Sensorineural Hearing Loss
Autoimmune: rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, vasculitis Bacterial: meningitis, Lyme disease, syphilis Medications: loop diuretics, aminoglycosides, erythromycin, antimalarial medications, some chemotherapy agents, possibly phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors Neoplasm: acoustic neuroma, leukemia/lymphoma, others Noise induced (gradual, often occupational exposure) Presbycusis Trauma: head/ear injury (falls, motor vehicle accidents), sudden noise (gunshot, explosions, etc.), barotrauma (SCUBA diving/airplane) Vascular: transient ischemic attack/stroke (especially vertebrobasilar/cerebellar) Viral: herpes viruses, HIV, measles, mumps, rubella, Influenza, enterovirus Other causes: hypothyroidism, Paget's disease of bone, multiple sclerosis, Ménière's disease, idiopathic Conductive Hearing Loss Cerumen impaction Cholesteatoma Congenital malformation Foreign body Middle ear effusion Osteoma Otitis externa Otitis media Otosclerosis Tumors (benign or malignant) Tympanic membrane perforation Based on case reports, there is a potential link between phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (used for erectile dysfunction and pulmonary artery hypertension) and sudden sensorineural hearing loss; withdrawal of the drug resolves or improves hearing loss in some.
